KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Maze — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches maze solving — the quiet game where the finger is the hero and every dead end is a clue.

What is this?

A maze is a path puzzle: travel from START to FINISH through the winding walls without crossing them.

What does it mean?

Solving a maze trains looking ahead, holding a plan, and calmly backing up from a dead end — resilience practice disguised as a puzzle.

What does the child need to know?

You need a maze (the card has one, and so does every activity book) and a finger — a pencil once the route is known.

Why this matters

Mazes are the quietest game on the shelf, and the win — reaching the FINISH star — is entirely the solver’s own.

What it teaches

Visual tracking, planning ahead one turn at a time, fine-motor tracing, and the patience of the wrong turn.

Words to learn

mazepathwalldead endtraceSTARTFINISH

Say this to your child

“"Finger on START... go slowly... this way... oops — a dead end! Back up, try the other path... there is the FINISH star! You solved it!"”

Step by step

  1. Find the START arrow and put a finger on it.
  2. Move slowly along the path — the finger is the traveler.
  3. Meet a fork? Look ahead at both paths — pick the one that goes further.
  4. Dead end? No problem — back the finger up and take the other path. Every dead end teaches the map.
  5. Reach the FINISH star — then trace the winning route again, fast, like a victory lap.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the maze has a START arrow, a FINISH star and one path already drawn through the purple walls — the drawn line is the route a brave finger took.

Ask your child

"Where does the path start?" "What do we do at a dead end?" (back up and try another path) "Can you find a shorter way than my finger took?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might solve it with two fingers racing each other, draw their own maze for you with three villainous dead ends, or refuse all help and solve it alone three times.

Out in the real world

Mazes wait in every activity book, every restaurant kids’ menu and every cereal box back — the finger-tracing practice is also the pencil-control practice school will ask for.

Try it together

Draw-your-own round: make a maze for someone else, with dead ends drawn on purpose — that is half the art. Timer round for fives: solve it before a slow count of thirty.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does every maze begin?" (at START) "What is a dead end?" (a path with no way through) "What do we do there?" (back up and try another way)

This lesson pairs with the Maze flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.
